cells.tense: You are carrying what was handed to you, and you have not lost your shape doing it.
cells.ask: Add one thing to what gets passed on — a recipe in your own handwriting, a step in the ritual nobody wrote down — and let it stand as yours.
cells.core:
You're holding something that got passed down to you, and you're doing it without hardening around it. Pressure comes and you don't grip harder and you don't put it down — the thing stays whole and usable in your hands.

The part worth noticing is that it doesn't read as strain from outside. It reads as care. What this balance can feed next is contact — letting the people who carry it alongside you know you're carrying it too, not as a report but as a fact of the room. Keeping it up costs something. You're the one paying, so you're the one who gets to say so.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it whole, and keeping it whole is still yours.
cells.verb: holding form under pressure without forcing it
cells.place: in what a family or a community hands down and keeps doing

cells.tense: You are bracing against a moment that has not arrived, standing guard before anyone asked you to.
cells.ask: Let one thing you're guarding run a week without your hand on it, and watch what holds without you.
cells.core:
You've got both hands on this, and you're holding harder than it needs. Somewhere ahead you can see it going wrong — the custom dropped, someone getting it wrong, the meaning quietly lost — and you're stiff against that already, so your grip tightens before there's anything to grip.

Strength turns into rigidity this way. Keeping it stops being a service and starts being a test of whether people will do it your way, and what the strength was for slips out of view while you enforce it. Loosening here isn't dropping it. It's letting the thing you've been carrying prove it stands without you, and finding out what your hands are for when they're not clamped.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding it so hard it stops being yours to pass on.

cells.tense: You set it down and stepped back, and you have not picked it up since.
cells.ask: Pick up one small piece of it this week — a single habit, one story you know by heart — and carry just that, no more.
cells.core:
The strength is there and you're not in the room anymore. You know what it takes to hold something and hand it on, and you've stepped back from the work of it — safer that way, easier, and nobody made you come back.

So the weight got set down and nobody replaced you. What's left is looking at it from outside: you can see the tradition, you care about it, you talk about it in the past tense. Coming back doesn't mean taking the whole thing. It means one piece, small enough that it won't flatten you, held long enough to find out you can still do it.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down to protect yourself. It's still sitting there.

cells.tense: You are already holding part of what gets passed down, and you call it just being the one who shows up.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person in it with you, that this matters to you — one sentence, no speech.
cells.core:
You're the one who keeps showing up — the meal, the call, the way the thing gets done right because you're doing it. That's holding. That's the strength here, running quietly, and you talk about it like it happens to you rather than through you.

What you're actually doing is keeping something alive between people, and if you were asked, you'd probably credit the occasion or the habit or the fact that someone has to. The strength is real and it's yours, and the not-claiming it is the only thing between you and it landing as what it is. Naming it isn't boasting. It's the difference between carrying and being seen to carry, which is the whole point of holding anything for other people.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive and call it just showing up.
